Abstract
Background
This study investigates whether ovarian structural and hormonal changes over a 13-year period differ between women diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and healthy controls within an unselected population.
Methods
This prospective nested cohort study followed up on a prevalence study conducted in 2009 in an unselected-population. A total of 41 women with PCOS (≥ 35 years-old, diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria) and 43 age- and body-mass-index-(BMI)-matched healthy controls were included from this cohort. The relationship between ovarian structure and hormonal profiles was tracked over 13 years. Antral follicle count (AFC) and ovarian volume (OV) were assessed by transvaginal/pelvic ultrasonography. Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), total testosterone (TT), sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), free androgen index (FAI), and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) were measured. The cardiometabolic profile of these aging women in same cohort was reported in a recent study.
Results
The mean age (44.1 ± 6.5 vs. 46.4 ± 4.2 years,
p
= 0.06), BMI (24.7; IQR:21.9–27.8 vs. 25.2; IQR:23.2–28.9,
p
= 0.16), and proportion of women in postmenopausal stage (75.6% vs. 62.8%,
p
= 0.24) were comparable between PCOS and control groups. Ovarian volume and AFC were significantly higher in the aging women with PCOS. At 13 years follow-up, PCOS group experienced a greater decline in AFC, AMH, and TT but retained higher levels of AMH, TT, FAI, and DHEAS than controls. An AMH cutoff of 1.17 ng/mL showed moderate diagnostic reliability for diagnosing PCOS in aging women, with an area under curve of 0.71 (95% CI:0.60–0.83).
Conclusions
Aging women with PCOS show greater declines in AFC, OV, AMH, and TT but maintain higher ovarian and hormonal levels than controls. Serum AMH provides moderate diagnostic utility for diagnosing PCOS in aging women.

Highlights
• The significant differences in the clinical and biochemical profiles between reproductive age PCOS and healthy control groups appear to diminish with advancing age.
• Aging women with PCOS exhibit higher levels of OV and AFC than aging healthy women.
• A cut-off for AMH value could be used at a moderate reliability level, helping in the diagnosis of PCOS in aging women.
• Both clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism findings are still more pronounced in aging women with PCOS when compared to aging healthy women.

Background
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine and metabolic disorder that can be found in 10% of reproductive-age women [
1
]. The diagnosis is made in the early reproductive age when any two of the following three criteria are present: oligo- or anovulation (OD), hyperandrogenism (HA) (biochemical and/or clinical), and a polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) [
2
,
3
].
Hyperandrogenemia is confirmed by elevated serum-free and/or total testosterone, with possible increases in androstenedione, DHEA, and DHEA-S, and manifests as hirsutism, acne, and androgenic alopecia. Ovulatory dysfunction affects 60–85% of cases, primarily as oligo- or amenorrhea, while polymenorrhagia is rare (~ < 2%). The presence of PCOM (antral follicle count per ovary > 20 when an 8 MHz vaginal probe is used or ovarian volume > 10 mm³) serves as a diagnostic criterion, particularly for women with mild symptoms and no significant hyperandrogenism [
4
,
5
]. PCOS is classified into four distinct phenotypes: A (HA + OD + PCOM), B (HA + OD), C (HA + PCOM), and D (OD + PCOM), which collectively account for 40–45% of cases, 35% of cases, 15% of cases, and 20% of cases, respectively. Higher referral rates for phenotypes A and B, which present with more severe hirsutism and obesity, may contribute to selection bias in PCOS studies of unselected populations [
6
,
7
].
Diagnosis of PCOS becomes difficult in late reproductive age and during the menopausal period. The course of the disease in menopause is still not fully understood. Women with PCOS have more primary follicles in the perimenopausal period than healthy women [
2
,
8
,
9
]. Studies have shown that serum testosterone level decreases with advancing age [
2
,
10
]. In addition, PCOM disappears with age, and oligo-anovulation symptoms are improved [
2
,
10
]—increased endometrial cancer rates found in perimenopausal PCOS patients [
2
,
5
]. There is no well-defined menopausal PCOS phenotype, yet. Moreover, the effect of menopausal transition on metabolic and psychologic long-term consequences is not well defined [
11
]. In the same cohort, we have recently reported that aging women with PCOS show a similar cardiometabolic risk profile to age- and BMI-matched healthy women in an unselected population [
12
]. Additionally, we found that epicardial fat thickness, a marker of cardiometabolic risk, is associated with body mass index (BMI), free androgen index (FAI) total and truncal body fat, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) [
12
].
Increased levels of anti-Mullerian Hormone (AMH) are observed in PCOS due to the increase in the number of secondary, preantral, and antral follicles [
13
] as a glycoprotein hormone released from the granulosa cells of those follicles. In the most recent guidelines, AMH has been proposed as an alternative to ultrasound for defining PCOM [
5
]. Cross-sectional follow-up data from selected or clinical cohorts are available on AMH and ultrasound in PCOS [
14
–
20
]. However, no prospective follow-up data exist on alterations in AMH and ovarian morphology in unselected populations. Given the significant variation in referral and unselected populations regarding PCOS diagnosis and phenotypes at younger ages [
7
], it is highly relevant and important to assess these alterations in the general population.
The objective of this study is to examine the ovarian structural and hormonal changes that occurred during a 13-year follow-up period in a group of women with PCOS in an unselected population. This study will also test whether serum AMH can assist in diagnosing PCOS in aging women and facilitate earlier intervention in conditions potentially related to a history of PCOS.
Materials methods
Study design and population
This study was designed as a prospective nested cohort study with a 13-year follow-up, conducted among female employees of the General Directorate of Mineral Research and Exploration (MTA) [
21
]. Details of the initial recruitment and evaluation of the PCOS and control groups have been reported previously [
12
].
In the original cohort, 392 unselected women were assessed between December 2009 and April 2010 [
21
]. Of these, 78 were diagnosed with PCOS according to the Rotterdam criteria. Among the remaining participants, 18 exhibited isolated oligo/anovulation, 37 exhibited isolated hyperandrogenism, and 69 exhibited isolated polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM). The remaining 190 women met none of these criteria and were classified as healthy controls. The present study is a follow-up of this cohort, aiming to evaluate the long-term effects of aging in women with PCOS compared to healthy controls.
For the follow-up, only women over 35 years of age at the time of re-evaluation were considered eligible. Among the 68 women with PCOS who met this criterion, 41 were successfully contacted and agreed to participate, forming the PCOS study group. Of the 183 eligible healthy controls, 43 women agreed to participate, comprising the control group. (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1).
Participants with FSH levels > 25 IU/L and no menstruation in the past year were classified as postmenopausal. The remaining participants—women over the age of 35 who continued to menstruate—are referred to as “late reproductive stage women” throughout the manuscript.
The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Hacettepe University, Ankara, Turkey (Project Number: GO-21/1201), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
Study protocol
Blood samples for hormonal and metabolic assessments of women with PCOS and healthy individuals were obtained in the early follicular phase (between the 3rd and 5th days of the menstrual cycle) from those who had not yet entered menopause. The samples were collected after at least 8 h of fasting, between 8:00 and 10:00 in the morning. For participants who had entered menopause, morning measurements after an 8-hour fasting period were taken on any given day.
Ultrasonographic assessment
All participants underwent ultrasound scanning on Days 2–7 of their menstrual bleeding. According to marital status, endocavitary (5–9 MHz) or abdominal (2–7 MHz) probe was preferred to calculate the estimated ovarian volume and AFC in which all procedures were performed by a single physician (N.C.S.). After obtaining three measurements for maximal longitudinal (a), transverse (b), and anteroposterior (c) dimensions, the over volume was calculated using the formula axbxcx0.5. The number of follicles observed in the transverse section of the ovary, ranging from 2 to 10 mm, was recorded as the antral follicle count.
Laboratory measurements
To assess hormonal status, levels of total testosterone, androstenedione, FSH, LH, DHEAS, SHBG, and AMH were determined in the basal serum in 2009. FSH, LH, total testosterone, DHEAS, and SHBG levels were measured using commercial assays as previously described [
21
,
22
]. DHEAS was assessed with Roche Diagnostics (Cobas) at baseline and Siemens Healthineers (Immulite) after follow-up, with comparable results to LC-MS/MS reported (Büttler RM. et al., 2013). Free androgen index (FAI) was calculated according to the standard accepted equation (FAI= [Total Testosterone (mmol/L)/SHBG (nmol/L)×100].
The previous investigation conducted that Immulite and Siemens Healthineers assays correlate with liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) measurements. Initial AMH levels of frozen serum aliquots from 84 women were used in a prevalence study conducted after following the manufacturer’s protocol for a single freeze-thaw procedure (Elecsys AMH; Roche Diagnostic International, IN, USA). The minimum detectable concentration was 0.01 ng/ml, the upper level of quantification was 23.0 ng/ml and the inter- and intra-assay coefficients of variation were 2.1% and 2.9%, respectively. The conversion factor for pmol/l was 7.14. Evaluations conducted after a 13-year follow-up were performed using the chemiluminescence method on the Beckman Coulter Unicel DxI800 hormone analyzer.
Statistical analyses
The categorical variables in the obtained data were described with percentages, while numerical variables were defined using median and ratio after determining whether the numerical variables followed a normal distribution. The normal distribution of the data was examined using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. In analyzing the relationship between categorical and numerical variables, the Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test was initially used for independent groups, and paired t-test or Wilcoxon test was used for dependent groups. For multiple comparisons, ANOVA test assuming normality in independent groups and Kruskal-Wallis test in non-normally distributed groups were employed. The relationships between categorical variables were examined using the chi-square test. A significance level of
p
< 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to calculate the threshold value. To determine the threshold AMH concentrations for PCOS diagnosis, those with at least 90% specificity were chosen to avoid the false positives in the controls. Statistical Packages for the Social Sciences v23.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL) software was utilized for statistical analysis.

p
= 0.06). Participants did not have a significant difference between their body weights and BMIs (Table
